::: {.chapter-lead}
This path connects conceptual explanations to the gradual construction of a small decoder-only GPT. **You do not need to master linear algebra, tensor calculus, or differential calculus beforehand.** The required operations are introduced when they become useful; broader mathematical treatments remain available as optional deep dives.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
**New to LLMs?** Start with the [LLM panorama](llm-overview.qmd) to distinguish model families and their lifecycle. This practical path then focuses on a decoder-only GPT.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
**Project status.** The route and conceptual pages are available, but the repository does not yet contain a complete, tested GPT implementation or a reproducible end-to-end training run. The milestones below distinguish existing knowledge from practical work that remains to be built.
:::

## The principle: learn only what is needed, when it is needed

At each milestone, distinguish:

- **Understand:** the mechanism and its role in the model.
- **Build:** the Python/PyTorch operation to implement and test.
- **Deepen:** optional theory that explains the mechanism more generally.

You need to read a tensor shape to debug an operation, not master tensor theory. You need to understand what a gradient represents before training, not complete a full course in differential calculus.


## Two paths that share the same model

Distinguish **inference** (using existing parameters to produce a token) from **learning** (changing those parameters from examples and a loss objective). These are not interchangeable descriptions of one loop.

::: {.callout-tip title="Why start with inference?"}
You can understand what a model does before studying how it was trained: first observe generation with fixed parameters, then ask where those parameters came from and how they are learned. In the build path, the first generation demonstration can use a randomly initialized GPT; its output will generally be incoherent. This separates **the mechanics of generation** from **the quality acquired through learning**. A useful model requires training or loading pretrained weights.
:::

### Generation path: from tokens to the next token

1. The tokenizer maps text to token IDs.
2. The embedding table maps those IDs to vectors; positional information is added or incorporated according to the architecture.
3. Transformer blocks transform these representations. Causal attention lets each position use its permitted context without accessing future tokens.
4. The output projection produces one logit per vocabulary token. Softmax can turn these scores into a conditional distribution.
5. A decoding rule selects the next token; it is appended to the context and the computation repeats.

**Be able to explain:** why the model predicts one token at a time, why logits are not probabilities, and why causal masking is needed. Parameters remain fixed during this generation process.

This loop and the rules for selecting the next token are detailed on the [Generating text: inference step by step](generation.qmd) page.

### Learning path: from examples to parameter updates

1. Prepare input sequences and shifted targets: at position (t), the model should predict the expected token at (t+1).
2. Run the model forward to obtain logits.
3. The loss compares logits with targets, respecting alignment and any ignored positions.
4. Backpropagation computes loss gradients with respect to the parameters.
5. An optimizer uses those gradients to update parameters; validation and monitoring help detect regressions and overfitting.

**Be able to explain:** the loss defines the objective, the gradient describes a local change in that objective, and the optimizer applies an update rule. Computing a gradient does not, by itself, guarantee better generalization.

Both paths use largely the same model computation. Their essential difference is what happens with the outputs: **generate with fixed parameters**, or **evaluate a loss and then update parameters**. Complete generation from a checkpoint and reproducible training remain practical deliverables to be built in this repository.

## What each milestone should let you verify

Concept pages are resources for reaching these outcomes; they are not evidence that the corresponding implementation already exists. Before moving on, the learner should be able to produce or verify the item below.

| Step | Observable expected outcome |
|---|---|
| Text and tokenization | Encode and decode a short text; identify the effects of special tokens and tokenizer version. |
| Embeddings and position | Trace shapes from `[B, L]` to `[B, L, D]` and explain each axis. |
| Causal attention | With the model in evaluation mode (dropout disabled), verify on a small example that changing a future token does not change earlier-position outputs, with parameters and earlier context held fixed. |
| GPT block | Trace dimensions through attention, residuals, normalization, MLP, and output projection; check parameter-count consistency. |
| Prediction and decoding | Distinguish logits from probabilities; explain greedy or sampled next-token selection. |
| Generation before training | Run the loop with random parameters and observe that the output is not yet coherent; check stopping and context limits. |
| Training examples | Construct an input window and its shifted target; test boundaries, padding, and separation between data splits. This branch is needed for learning, not for generation. |
| Loss and training | Align logits/targets, calculate the loss, reproduce a small update, and track training and validation losses separately. |
| Generation after training | Load a trained checkpoint and compare outputs under documented decoding conditions. |
| Evaluation | Compare against a baseline under an explicit protocol; analyze errors and state what the metrics do not establish. |

These criteria are **learning outcomes**, not a change in repository status: an available page, a hand-checkable example, an automated test, a reproducible run, and visual review are different levels of evidence.

## Build milestones

| Step | What you build | Concept pages | Practical status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0. Define the model | Place LLM families, then scope the decoder-only GPT studied here and its objective | [LLM panorama](llm-overview.qmd), [GPT / Transformer overview](transformer.qmd), [history](transformer-history.qmd) as optional context | **Conceptual material available** — the broad panorama and the scope of the selected GPT are documented; the complete executable model remains to be built |
| 1. Prepare text input | Understand the tokenizer and encode/decode a prompt; corpus construction belongs to the training branch | [Text and data](text-data.qmd), [Unicode](unicode-text.qmd), [tokenization](tokenization-strategies.qmd) | **Conceptual** — no complete, validated tokenizer pipeline is established in the repository |
| 2. Represent tokens | Embedding lookup and positional information | [Embedding space](embedding-space.qmd), [position](positional-encoding.qmd) | **Conceptual** — no validated complete GPT embedding stack |
| 3. Compute attention | Q/K/V projections, scores, softmax and causal mask | [Q/K/V](queries-keys-values.qmd), [attention](scaled-dot-product-attention.qmd), [causal masking](causal-masking.qmd) | **Conceptual** — mechanisms are documented; the complete module and tests remain to be built |
| 4. Assemble GPT | Transformer blocks, residuals, normalization, MLP and output projection | [Transformer](transformer.qmd), [tensors](tensors.qmd) as needed | **Partial** — system overview exists; a complete configurable and tested model does not |
| 5. Predict and select | Logits, probabilities and the decoding rule | [Logits](logits.qmd), [probabilities](probabilities.qmd), [Transformer](transformer.qmd), [generation step by step](generation.qmd) | **Partial** — concepts are explained; full integration into generation remains to be built |
| 6. Generate before training | Run the autoregressive loop with the assembled GPT's random parameters; observe untrained output | [Transformer](transformer.qmd), [logits](logits.qmd), [probabilities](probabilities.qmd), [generation step by step](generation.qmd) | **To build** — complete demonstration and stopping/context tests are absent |
| 7. Prepare training data | Documented and partitioned corpus; context windows, shifted inputs/targets, batches and masks | [Text and data](text-data.qmd), [training examples](training-examples.qmd) | **Conceptual** — rules and pitfalls are explained; the complete executable pipeline remains to be established |
| 8. Train and validate | Loss, backpropagation, optimizer, validation and checkpoints | [Cross-entropy](cross-entropy.qmd), [loss](loss.qmd), [gradients](gradients.qmd), [evaluation](experimental-evaluation.qmd) | **To build** — no reproducible end-to-end GPT training run |
| 9. Evaluate | Baselines, metrics, error analysis and limitations | [Experimental evaluation](experimental-evaluation.qmd) | **Method available** — no complete evaluation of a locally trained GPT |

Detailed prerequisites, expected evidence, dependencies and validation criteria are maintained in the [versioned build plan](https://github.com/JM-Brun/llm-lab/blob/main/docs/learning-path.md).

## Knowledge to acquire along the way

| Topic | Minimum useful for building | Optional deeper study |
|---|---|---|
| Tensors | Read `[B, L]`, `[B, L, D]`, `[B, L, V]` and check the axes used | General tensor algebra, advanced broadcasting, conventions and properties |
| Linear algebra | Understand a projection and matrix product in the dimensions encountered | Vector spaces, bases, spectra, operators and proofs |
| Probability | Understand a categorical distribution and softmax | Probability and information theory |
| Derivatives and gradients | Understand local sensitivity and use automatic differentiation | Detailed chain rule, Jacobians and numerical optimization |
| Optimization | Understand the role of learning rate and optimizer | Convergence, conditioning, adaptive methods and advanced analysis |

**Do not confuse this educational project with industrial-scale training.** A small randomly initialized GPT makes transformations and errors inspectable. It does not reproduce the data volumes, compute resources, or performance of a production LLM.
